According to ritual propriety, men and women are kept distinct so as to make clear the avoidance of suspicion; would he then so readily converse with a woman out in the fields and countryside? The Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji) records that when Nanzi of Wei summoned Confucius for an audience, she bowed twice from behind a fine linen curtain, herjade pendants and rings tinkling clearly—this is truly an actual deed of Confucius. Yet Han Ying claims that when Confucius was traveling in Agu, upon seeing an unmarried girl wearing ear-ornaments and washing clothes, he drew out a goblet and a zither, handed them to Zigong, and had him speak with her. Now, because the Odes (Shi) contain many words spoken by women, Han in explaining the Odes wished to attribute them to a woman and borrow Confucius to lend them credence; yet how base and vulgar these words are! That he studied the zither with Music Master Xiang (Shi Xiang) is recorded in tradition; yet it goes so far as to say that after a long time he saw a man there—dark in complexion, tall in stature, with eyes gazing afar and a mind set on the four quarters—whereupon Xiang stepped off his mat, bowed twice, and said, “This is the melody of King Wen!” How absurd that is! The saying goes, “When thought is concentrated to the utmost, the form takes shape”—could it really mean something like this? That he ascended to the summit of Mount Tai is recorded in tradition; yet when it goes so far as to say that he gazed out and saw a white horse tethered outside the Chang Gate of Wu, and drew Yan Hui forward to ask him about it, to which Hui replied, “I see it as though it were a bolt of white silk”—this is the height of absurdity! The saying goes, “Sight that does not rely on looking can see ten thousand li”—surely it does not mean this. As for using a six-foot staff to distinguish the degrees of kinship and distance, this account is found in the Spring and Autumn of Master Lü (Lüshi chunqiu) and Jia Yi's New Writings (Xinshu), which say that when Zigong came from his home, Confucius raised his staff, bent his waist like a chiming stone, and inquired after his parents; then laid down his staff and inquired after his brothers; and then dragged his staff…

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
而問其妻子吾意聖人教人自有章程而
必爲是狀者毋乃勞而不情乎一飯之桃
以定貴賤之等其說具家語新序中謂魯
公以黍雪桃孔子侍食則先啗黍曰君子
不以貴承賤吾謂聖人誠不可則當謝罷
不食直告之故耳奚待左右之人掩口而
笑而後發其旨也原壤登木而歌大故也
乃爲弗聞也者而過之而曰親者毋失其
爲親故者毋失其爲故信也其友誼之謂
===
何必不然矣陳恒篡齊大變也第聲大義
以討之可矣而曰齊民之不與者半以魯
之衆加齊之半可克也校量於衆寡之間
豈聖人之言耶春秋書災異而不書應乃
魯廟災謂孔子在陳聞之嘆曰其桓僖乎
彼其親盡不毁也而其言卒驗當術數之
學聖人不道也子張問十世可知但以因
革損益推之奚爲書誡其後曰不知何一
男子名秦始皇上我堂恐讖緯之書聖人
punctuated: 而問其妻子。吾意聖人教人，自有章程，而必爲是狀者，毋乃勞而不情乎？一飯之桃以定貴賤之等，其說具《家語》、《新序》中，謂魯公以黍雪桃，孔子侍食，則先啗黍，曰：「君子不以貴承賤。」吾謂聖人誠不可，則當謝罷不食，直告之故耳，奚待左右之人掩口而笑，而後發其旨也？原壤登木而歌，大故也，乃爲弗聞也者而過之，而曰：「親者毋失其爲親，故者毋失其爲故。」信也，其友誼之謂何？必不然矣。陳恒篡齊，大變也，第聲大義以討之可矣，而曰：「齊民之不與者半，以魯之衆加齊之半，可克也。」校量於衆寡之間，豈聖人之言耶？《春秋》書災異而不書應，乃魯廟災，謂孔子在陳聞之，嘆曰：「其桓、僖乎！」彼其親盡不毁也，而其言卒驗。當術數之學，聖人不道也。子張問十世可知，但以因革損益推之，奚爲書誡其後曰：「不知何一男子，名秦始皇，上我堂」？恐讖緯之書，聖人
translation_en:
… and asked after his wife and children. In my opinion, the Sage had his own established principles for instructing people; to insist on acting out such postures—would that not be tiresome and unnatural?

As for using peaches at a single meal to determine the hierarchy of noble and base, this account appears in the Kongzi jiayu (School Sayings of Confucius) and the Xinxu (New Arrangements). It claims that Duke Ai of Lu offered millet to wipe the fuzz off peaches, and Confucius, attending the meal, ate the millet first, saying, "A gentleman does not use the noble to serve the base." In my view, if the Sage truly found this improper, he ought simply to have declined and not eaten, stating the reason directly. Why wait until the attendants covered their mouths and laughed before revealing his point?

When Yuan Rang 原壤 climbed atop the coffin wood and sang during a great bereavement, Confucius supposedly passed by pretending not to hear, saying, "Kinsmen should not lose their kinship; old friends should not lose their old friendship." If one truly took this to be so, what would that say of the righteousness of friendship? It was certainly not the case.

When Chen Heng 陳恒 usurped power in Qi, it was a great calamity. It would have sufficed simply to proclaim great righteousness and launch a punitive expedition against him. Yet it is claimed Confucius said, "Half the people of Qi do not support him; if we add the multitude of Lu to half of Qi, he can be overcome." Calculating the relative numbers of many and few—how could those be the words of the Sage?

The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) records disasters and prodigies without recording their retributive correspondences. Yet when the ancestral temples of Lu caught fire, it is said that Confucius heard of it while in Chen and sighed, "Was it not the temples of Huan and Xi!"—because the kinship obligations to them had expired, yet their shrines had not been demolished—and that his words ultimately proved true. That belongs to the art of prognostication and numerology, which the Sage did not speak of. When Zizhang 子張 asked whether ten generations hence could be known, Confucius deduced it solely through what is inherited, reformed, added to, and subtracted from in ritual. Why then would he leave a written warning for posterity saying, "I know not what man, named First Emperor of Qin (Qin Shihuang 秦始皇), will ascend my hall"? I fear that books of prophecy and apocrypha are things the Sage …

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
不爲也萍實徵霸商羊占雨奚皆使人問
于孔子乎猶亡足異也至宋人黑牛生白
犢此何吉祥哉而命以薦上帝則幾于語
怪矣毋亦東方朔射覆者之流託言之乎
土之怪曰羵羊防風氏之骨專車又奚皆
問于孔子知之乎此猶足信也至謂有隼
集于陳侯之庭貫楛矢石砮其長尺有咫
曰肅愼氏之矢也抑何不經之甚耶或者
多識如張茂先之流爲之也大都尊孔子
===
者欲加以神明多智之稱則爲童謠遺讖
之說而妬孔子者卽又置問發難如小兒
辯日之類欲以詘孔子而謂聖人徒有所
不知是皆竅言也是皆善亂聖人之眞者
也距之則息而揚之復焰核其實則悖而
聽其言則美恐鄭亂雅屏去其書不觀者
實鮮而以雅爲鄭又從而啑囈之掎角之
者則什家而九也亦奚足怪哉故曰取摶
黍與十金以示小兒則小兒必取摶黍矣取
punctuated: 不爲也。萍實徵霸、商羊占雨，奚皆使人問于孔子乎？猶亡足異也。至宋人黑牛生白犢，此何吉祥哉？而命以薦上帝，則幾于語怪矣。毋亦東方朔射覆者之流託言之乎？土之怪曰羵羊，防風氏之骨專車，又奚皆問于孔子知之乎？此猶足信也。至謂有隼集于陳侯之庭，貫楛矢石砮，其長尺有咫，曰「肅愼氏之矢也」，抑何不經之甚耶！或者多識如張茂先之流爲之也。大都尊孔子者，欲加以神明多智之稱，則爲童謠遺讖之說；而妬孔子者，卽又置問發難，如小兒辯日之類，欲以詘孔子，而謂聖人徒有所不知。是皆竅言也，是皆善亂聖人之眞者也。距之則息，而揚之復焰；核其實則悖，而聽其言則美。恐鄭亂雅，屏去其書不觀者實鮮；而以雅爲鄭，又從而啑囈之、掎角之者，則什家而九也，亦奚足怪哉！故曰：取摶黍與十金以示小兒，則小兒必取摶黍矣；取
translation_en:
… would not do. Why is it that for the duckweed fruit signifying hegemonic rule and the one-legged shangyang bird foretelling rain, people were in every case sent to ask Confucius? Even so, those are hardly worth marveling at. As for a black cow of a man of Song giving birth to a white calf—what auspicious omen was this? Yet to command that it be offered in sacrifice to the Lord on High comes close to speaking of prodigies! Was this not fabricated and attributed to him by the likes of Dongfang Shuo (東方朔), who practiced guessing objects hidden under bowls? That the monstrosity of the earth is called the fenyang (羵羊) sheep-spirit, and that a single bone of the Fangfeng (防風) clan filled an entire cart—why again did everyone know of these only by asking Confucius? Even these might still be credible. But when it comes to the claim that a falcon alighted in the courtyard of the Marquis of Chen, pierced by a hushi (楛矢) wooden arrow with a stone arrowhead measuring a foot and eight inches in length, and that he said, "This is an arrow of the Sushen (肅愼) clan"—how utterly preposterous and uncanonical that is! Perhaps men of wide learning like Zhang Maoxian (張茂先, Zhang Hua 張華) and his sort concocted it.

On the whole, those who revered Confucius wished to bestow upon him the reputation of godlike illumination and vast wisdom, and so they invented stories of children's rhymes and leftover prophecies; whereas those who envied Confucius in turn posed questions and raised objections—such as the tale of the two children debating the distance of the sun—wishing to stump Confucius and claim that the Sage merely had things he did not know. These are all empty, specious words; these are all things adept at confounding the true nature of the Sage. If one resists them, they subside, yet if one fans them, they flare up again; if one examines their reality, they are perverse, yet if one listens to their words, they sound appealing. Those who fear that the tunes of Zheng will confound the elegant music (ya) and therefore cast aside such books without reading them are truly few; whereas those who take the elegant for the郑 (Zheng), and furthermore chatter away about them in their sleep and join forces to champion them, make up nine out of ten schools! What is there to wonder at in this? Therefore it is said: If you take a ball of glutinous millet and ten pieces of gold to show a small child, the small child will certainly take the ball of millet; if you take …

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
十金與道德之言以示庸眾人則庸眾人
必取十金矣後之人率持兒于庸眾之見
所取彌埆如魯論鄉黨諸篇孔子言語行
事之實大中至正之道往往屑越之如遺
至於列子稱力拓北門之關王充論衡稱
有百觚之量淮南子稱智過萇弘足躡郊
菟也則爭引以薦談申申夭夭之容可想
見也而乃亟述其東門纍纍之誚豈無誦
其江漢秋陽之盛美也而不多於麕裘無
===
戾之歌日與七十子講藝杏壇之上濟濟
雍雍弗稱也而商也以假蓋見疑參也以
受杖見斥輒置喙焉故曰天下有竅言則
聖人鮮真詮可慨也今人聞人呼其父祖
之名則艴然不悅設有詆詈之者且攘臂
前矣憂心悄悄慍于羣小無如吾孔子之
遭也此非後死者之責與昔季由見毀於
魏而誣孔子以自解子順勃然為爭諸魏
侯之前主侍人瘠環之謗孟子亟辭而斥
punctuated: 十金與道德之言以示庸眾人，則庸眾人必取十金矣。後之人率持兒于、庸眾之見，所取彌埆。如《魯論》〈鄉黨〉諸篇，孔子言語行事之實，大中至正之道，往往屑越之如遺；至於《列子》稱力拓北門之關，王充《論衡》稱有百觚之量，《淮南子》稱智過萇弘、足躡郊菟也，則爭引以薦談。申申夭夭之容可想見也，而乃亟述其東門纍纍之誚；豈無誦其江漢秋陽之盛美也，而不多於〈麕裘無戾〉之歌；日與七十子講藝杏壇之上，濟濟雍雍，弗稱也，而商也以假蓋見疑，參也以受杖見斥，輒置喙焉。故曰：天下有竅言，則聖人鮮真詮，可慨也！今人聞人呼其父祖之名，則艴然不悅；設有詆詈之者，且攘臂前矣。「憂心悄悄，慍于羣小」，無如吾孔子之遭也，此非後死者之責與？昔季由見毀於魏，而誣孔子以自解，子順勃然為爭諸魏侯之前；主侍人瘠環之謗，孟子亟辭而斥…
translation_en: … ten pieces of gold and words of morality to show to ordinary people, then ordinary people will surely take the ten pieces of gold. People of later times generally hold the views of children [?] and ordinary crowds, and what they choose to adopt becomes ever more barren and shallow. For instance, in chapters such as "Xiangdang" (Among the Xiang and Dang) in the Lu Analects (Lunyu), the true reality of Confucius's words and deeds—the Way of great centrality and utmost correctness—is often cast aside by them as if forgotten. Yet when it comes to the Liezi claiming that his strength could lift the bolt of the northern gate, Wang Chong's Balanced Discourses (Lunheng) claiming that he had the capacity for a hundred goblets of wine, or the Huainanzi claiming that his wisdom surpassed Chang Hong's and his feet could overtake a hare in the suburbs, they vie with one another to cite these to spice up their conversations. His relaxed and cheerful demeanor can easily be imagined, yet they eagerly recount the mockery of him looking as weary as a stray dog at the eastern gate. Is it that no one recites the resplendent beauty of his being washed by the Jiang and Han rivers and bleached by the autumn sun? Yet such recitations are not as numerous as the song of the "fawn-skin coat without fault" (Qunqiu wuli). That he daily discussed the arts with his seventy disciples upon the Apricot Altar, in an atmosphere dignified and harmonious, goes unmentioned; instead, whenever there is a tale like Bu Shang (Zixia) being suspected over borrowing a canopy, or Zeng Can (Zengzi) being rebuked for submitting to a beating with a staff, they are quick to chime in. Therefore it is said: when the world is full of specious words, there is rarely a true understanding of the Sage—how lamentable! Nowadays, if someone hears another person call out the personal name of his father or grandfather, he flushes with displeasure; and suppose someone were to slander or revile them, he would roll up his sleeves and step forward to fight. "My heart is anxious and sad; I am hated by the crowd of petty men"—nothing matches what our Confucius encountered. Is it not the responsibility of us who die later to defend him? In the past, when Ji You was criticized in Wei and falsely implicated Confucius to excuse himself, Zishun (Kong Bin) indignantly argued the matter before the Marquis of Wei; as for the slander that he stayed as a guest at the home of the eunuch Jihuan, Mencius urgently refuted and rejected…

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
之生也孔子之徒也卽執事者不以問二
三子固將講之
第三問
同考試官敎諭蕭批人才之難自古記之衡鏡
所在世道繫焉善哉子之言是
同考試官訓導魯批古稱才德非二道也後乃
科別之以為評品異矣此作得題旨宜錄
考試官學正陳批援古辨才皆繩尺語
===
考試官學正王批引據悉對爛然有第
今之譚才德者離其指矣夫天性之謂道
體道之謂德德應於物焉之謂才夫德内
以脩身外以治人以正君臣以親父子以
序兄弟長幼以順夫婦以成朋友之交以
辨庶政理萬物之宜天子用之以治天下
諸侯用之以治其國卿大夫用之以治其
官士庶人用之以治其家廣之塞宇宙窮
日月遠之施乎後世無出乎德者也大哉
punctuated:
之。生也，孔子之徒也，卽執事者不以問，二三子固將講之。

第三問
同考試官敎諭蕭批：人才之難，自古記之。衡鏡所在，世道繫焉。善哉，子之言是！
同考試官訓導魯批：古稱才德非二道也，後乃科別之以為評品，異矣。此作得題旨，宜錄。
考試官學正陳批：援古辨才，皆繩尺語。
考試官學正王批：引據悉對，爛然有第。

今之譚才德者，離其指矣。夫天性之謂道，體道之謂德，德應於物焉之謂才。夫德，内以脩身，外以治人，以正君臣，以親父子，以序兄弟長幼，以順夫婦，以成朋友之交，以辨庶政、理萬物之宜。天子用之以治天下，諸侯用之以治其國，卿大夫用之以治其官，士庶人用之以治其家。廣之塞宇宙、窮日月，遠之施乎後世，無出乎德者也。大哉！
translation_en:
… it. I, the candidate, am a follower of Confucius; even if Your Excellencies had not asked about this, we disciples would certainly have discussed it.

Third Question
Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Xiao: The difficulty of finding men of talent has been recorded since antiquity. Upon the balance and mirror of selection, the moral state of the world depends. Excellent! What you say on this is right.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Lu: In antiquity it was said that talent and virtue are not two separate ways; only later were they divided into distinct categories for evaluation and grading—how strange! This essay grasps the purport of the question and ought to be selected for inclusion.
Comment by Examiner and Director of Studies Chen: Citing antiquity to discriminate talent, every word conforms to the standard measure.
Comment by Examiner and Director of Studies Wang: The citations and proofs all correspond thoroughly to the questions, brilliantly arranged in orderly sequence.

Those who discuss talent and virtue today have departed from their essential meaning. Now, what is endowed by Heavenly nature is called the Way; embodying the Way is called virtue; and virtue responding to things is called talent. As for virtue, inwardly it is used to cultivate the self, and outwardly to govern others; to rectify the relation between ruler and minister, to foster affection between father and son, to order elder and younger brothers, to harmonize husband and wife, to perfect intercourse among friends, to distinguish the various affairs of administration, and to regulate what is fitting for the myriad things. The Son of Heaven uses it to govern All-under-Heaven; the feudal lords use it to govern their states; the grandees and great officers use it to govern their offices; and scholars and commoners use it to govern their families. Broadened, it fills the cosmos and reaches to the limits of the sun and moon; extended afar, it is bestowed upon later generations—there is nothing that goes beyond virtue. Great indeed, …

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
洋洋乎德之施也由斯以譚才藏之爲德
德徵之爲才德者才之統才者德之名可
以名之爲德亦可名之爲才非二物也請
以書記明之書稱高陽氏才子八人曰齊
聖廣淵明允篤誠高辛氏才子八人曰忠
肅恭懿宣慈惠和其所號爲才率皆德行
之稱而窮奇檮杌饕餮諸悖德者卽所謂
不才者也迺言九德曰寬而栗柔而立愿
而恭亂而敬擾而毅直而溫簡而廉剛而
===
塞彊而義類皆與才雜稱之而用之俊明
有家亮采有邦者卽九德也故當其時上
下咨美功業禹稷咎繇並以德著而仲尼
嘆才難五臣十亂皆以才稱蓋其指才德
一也善夫孟子之言性善也曰乃若其情
則可以爲善矣若夫爲不善非才之罪也
又曰富歲多賴凶歲多暴非天之降才殊
也吾是以明才者性之能也德也昔人蓋
並言之後之儒者不喻其指而徒睹其跡
punctuated: 洋洋乎德之施也！由斯以譚，才藏之爲德，德徵之爲才；德者，才之統，才者，德之名。可以名之爲德，亦可名之爲才，非二物也。請以書記明之：《書》稱高陽氏才子八人，曰「齊、聖、廣、淵、明、允、篤、誠」；高辛氏才子八人，曰「忠、肅、恭、懿、宣、慈、惠、和」。其所號爲才，率皆德行之稱；而窮奇、檮杌、饕餮諸悖德者，卽所謂不才者也。迺言九德，曰：「寬而栗，柔而立，愿而恭，亂而敬，擾而毅，直而溫，簡而廉，剛而塞，彊而義。」類皆與才雜稱之，而用之「俊明有家」、「亮采有邦」者，卽九德也。故當其時，上下咨美功業，禹、稷、咎繇並以德著；而仲尼嘆「才難」，五臣、十亂皆以才稱。蓋其指才德一也。善夫！孟子之言性善也，曰：「乃若其情，則可以爲善矣；若夫爲不善，非才之罪也。」又曰：「富歲多賴，凶歲多暴，非天之降才殊也。」吾是以明才者性之能也，德也，昔人蓋並言之。後之儒者不喻其指，而徒睹其跡，
translation_en: …and vast indeed is the application of virtue! Speaking from this perspective, when talent is stored within, it is virtue; when virtue is manifested externally, it is talent. Virtue is the totality of talent, and talent is the name given to virtue. One may name it virtue, or one may name it talent—they are not two separate things. Allow me to clarify this through historical records. Ancient writings state that the clan of Gaoyang (高陽氏) had eight talented sons, described as "orderly, sagely, broad-minded, profound, perceptive, trustworthy, sincere, and genuine"; and the clan of Gaoxin (高辛氏) had eight talented sons, described as "loyal, reverent, respectful, admirable,comprehensive, compassionate, benevolent, and harmonious." What was designated as "talent" here consisted entirely of terms for virtuous conduct; whereas those who rebelled against virtue—such as Qiongqi (窮奇), Taowu (檮杌), and Taotie (饕餮)—were precisely what were called the "untalented" (bucai 不才). Furthermore, in speaking of the Nine Virtues (jiude 九德), the Book of Documents says: "Affable yet dignified, mild yet firm, blunt yet respectful, apt for governance yet reverent, docile yet bold, straightforward yet gentle, easygoing yet discerning, rigid yet sincere, and strong yet righteous." All of these are referred to interchangeably with talent, and what were employed so that "men of eminent virtue would hold hereditary families" and "men of bright accomplishments would govern states" were none other than the Nine Virtues. Therefore, in those times, when ruler and ministers praised glorious achievements in counsel, Yu (禹), Ji (稷), and Gao Yao (咎繇) were all renowned for their virtue; yet when Confucius (Zhongni 仲尼) sighed that "talent is difficult to find," the five ministers of Shun and the ten capable ministers of King Wu were all praised for their talent. This is because, in their view, talent and virtue were one. How admirable are Mencius's (Mengzi 孟子) words on the goodness of human nature! He said: "As for our innate disposition, it is capable of doing good; if someone does what is not good, that is not the fault of their natural talent." He also said: "In good years the young men are mostly dependable; in bad years they are mostly violent. It is not that Heaven confers different talents upon them." From this I understand that talent is the capability of one's innate nature, and it is virtue; the ancients spoke of them together. Later scholars failed to grasp this meaning, and merely looked at their outward traces…

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
於是支離才德科列序途用以剽剝士林
考鏡失得其言犁然可喜而本之謬於初
指焉亢倉子曰賢可以正國才亦可以治
國賢者沈運無迹人不知其方才者勤率
其事人知所矜德一賢統衆才而有餘衆
才度一賢猶不足此尊德而卑才上德者
之所因也而顧未知德亦才也華丘游曰
事父母使家人稱孝孰與治官難束帶而
敎吏民使國人愛之孰與鼓三軍之士以
===
===
走强敵難故德可勉而才不可强此難才
而易德喜才者之所託也而惡知才即德
耶劉常侍有言偏至之才以才自名兼材
之人以德爲目兼德之人更爲美號兼德
而至謂之中庸具體而微謂之德行一至
謂之偏才一徵謂之依似一至一違謂之
間雜其指蓋以兼材爲大德一德爲偏材
而因廣其流焉淮南子曰天下不可以智
爲也不可以慧識也不可以事治也不可
punctuated: 於是支離才德，科列序途，用以剽剝士林，考鏡失得。其言犁然可喜，而本之謬於初指焉。亢倉子曰：「賢可以正國，才亦可以治國。賢者沈運無迹，人不知其方；才者勤率其事，人知所矜德。一賢統衆才而有餘，衆才度一賢猶不足。」此尊德而卑才，上德者之所因也，而顧未知德亦才也。華丘游曰：「事父母，使家人稱孝，孰與治官難？束帶而敎吏民，使國人愛之，孰與鼓三軍之士以走强敵難？故德可勉，而才不可强。」此難才而易德，喜才者之所託也，而惡知才即德耶？劉常侍有言：「偏至之才，以才自名；兼材之人，以德爲目；兼德之人，更爲美號。兼德而至，謂之中庸；具體而微，謂之德行；一至，謂之偏才；一徵，謂之依似；一至一違，謂之間雜。」其指蓋以兼材爲大德，一德爲偏材，而因廣其流焉。淮南子曰：「天下不可以智爲也，不可以慧識也，不可以事治也，不可
translation_en: …thereupon they severed talent from virtue, classifying them into ranks and paths, using this to dissect the community of scholars and examine their successes and failures. Their words are clear and pleasing, yet at their root they deviate from the original meaning. Master Gengsang (Kangcangzi 亢倉子) said: "Worthiness can rectify a state, and talent can also govern a state. A worthy person operates quietly without leaving a trace, so people do not know his methods; a talented person diligently leads in affairs, so people know for what to feel gratitude. One worthy person is more than enough to command a multitude of talents, whereas a multitude of talents is still insufficient to measure a single worthy person." This exalts virtue and disparages talent—it is what those who prize virtue rely upon, yet they fail to realize that virtue is also talent. Huaqiu You 華丘游 said: "Serving one's parents so that the household praises one's filial piety—how does that compare in difficulty with governing an office? Donning court sash and instructing subofficials and the common people so that the people of the state love one—how does that compare in difficulty with rallying the soldiers of the Three Armies to rout a powerful enemy? Therefore, virtue can be striven after, whereas talent cannot be forced." This treats talent as difficult and virtue as easy—it is the pretext of those who are fond of talent, yet how could they know that talent is none other than virtue? Regular Attendant Liu (Liu Shao 劉劭) had a saying: "Those of one-sided perfection in talent take 'talent' as their designation; those who combine multiple abilities take 'virtue' as their label; and those who combine virtues are given even finer titles. Combining virtues to perfection is called the Constant Mean; possessing the whole body of virtue in miniature is called 'virtuous conduct'; reaching perfection in one aspect is called 'one-sided talent'; showing a single token of it is called 'approximation'; reaching perfection in one respect while erring in another is called 'admixture.'" His point was probably to regard combined abilities as great virtue, and a single virtue as one-sided ability, and thereby broaden their categories. The Master of Huainan (Huainanzi 淮南子) said: "All under Heaven cannot be managed by cleverness, nor comprehended by shrewdness, nor governed by mere handling of affairs, nor…

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
以仁附也不可以强勝也五者皆才也德
不盛不能成一德立則五無殆五見而德
無位其指蓋謂才爲德之施德行乎才之
中而原本於德矣二子之言才德一貫吾
猶有取焉自後方人者乃爲之科曰某也
德某也才甲曰寧德勝才乙曰無寧才勝
德彼其稱量或有當乎而才德裂矣以彼
其言則抱德者何其不當於用而亡德之
人安所取才乎吾不知德何施而才又何
===
物也吾求其說而不得竊意者其毋乃後
世之所謂才德非古之才德乎管子能脫
檻車合諸侯以齊國富强而內行不脩不
能致王孔子小之吴起能修法令戰勝攻
取以張楚魏而刻覈積怨困於王錯詘於
田文蘇秦張儀用口舌以縱衡之䇿聲震
諸侯而押闔變詐智窮身及儒者羞而不
道何者彼所謂才者權數揣摩之智耳令
四子而古之才也安有而卑卑若是尾生
punctuated: 以仁附也，不可以强勝也。五者皆才也，德不盛，不能成一；德立則五無殆，五見而德無位。其指蓋謂才爲德之施，德行乎才之中，而原本於德矣。二子之言，才德一貫，吾猶有取焉。自後方人者乃爲之科曰：「某也德，某也才。」甲曰：「寧德勝才。」乙曰：「無寧才勝德。」彼其稱量或有當乎？而才德裂矣。以彼其言，則抱德者何其不當於用，而亡德之人安所取才乎？吾不知德何施，而才又何物也。吾求其說而不得，竊意者其毋乃後世之所謂才德，非古之才德乎？管子能脫檻車、合諸侯，以齊國富强，而內行不脩，不能致王，孔子小之；吴起能修法令、戰勝攻取，以張楚、魏，而刻覈積怨，困於王錯，詘於田文；蘇秦、張儀用口舌，以縱衡之䇿，聲震諸侯，而押闔變詐，智窮身及，儒者羞而不道。何者？彼所謂才者，權數揣摩之智耳。令四子而古之才也，安有而卑卑若是？尾生
translation_en:
… won over through benevolence alone, nor conquered by force alone. These five are all talents; if virtue is not abundant, not one of them can be brought to completion. When virtue is established, the five are free from peril; when the five merely show themselves on their own, virtue has no place." His point is蓋 that talent is the application of virtue, that virtue operates within talent, and that talent has its root in virtue. In the words of these two masters, talent and virtue form a single thread, and I still find something worth adopting in them.

Later on, those who evaluated people created separate categories for them, saying, "So-and-so has virtue; so-and-so has talent." One person says, "Better that virtue surpass talent," while another says, "Rather let talent surpass virtue." Even if their weighing and measuring might hit the mark in some cases, talent and virtue have thereby been torn apart! According to what they say, why would one who possesses virtue be so unsuited for practical use, and from where would a person devoid of virtue derive his talent? I would not know how virtue is applied, nor what sort of thing talent is. I sought an explanation for their view and could not find one; I privately suspect that what later ages call talent and virtue is simply not the talent and virtue of antiquity!

Master Guan (Guan Zhong 管仲) was able to step out of a prisoner's cart, assemble the feudal lords, and make the state of Qi rich and strong; yet his personal conduct was uncultivated and he could not bring about true kingly rule, so Confucius considered him of small capacity. Wu Qi 吳起 was able to reform laws and ordinances, win battles and conquer territory to expand the power of Chu and Wei; yet through his harshness he accumulated resentment, being thwarted by Wang Cuo 王錯 and outmaneuvered by Tian Wen 田文. Su Qin 蘇秦 and Zhang Yi 張儀 used their glib tongues and strategies of vertical and horizontal alliances to make their reputations resound among the feudal lords; yet with their manipulative maneuvering and deceitful shifts, when their wits were exhausted disaster befell their own persons, so Confucian scholars are ashamed even to speak of them. Why is this? What those men called "talent" was nothing more than the cleverness of tactical calculation and sizing up others. Suppose these four men possessed the talent of antiquity—how could it be so base and paltry as this? The trustworthiness of Weisheng 尾生…

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
之信也而愚子羔之孝也而愚孟公綽優
於趙魏老不可以爲滕薛大夫鮑叔牙忠
信廉潔而不可以託國當彼所謂德者顓
固曲方之行耳今四子而古之德也有不
可以大受者乎是故有伊尹傅說之德則
必能阿衡商業舟楫大川有周公之德則
必能勝殷遏劉朝委裘而致太平孔子曰
有德者必有言仁者必有勇又曰我戰則
克祭則受福故仕魯三月男女別于途道
===
不拾遺市不預價魯國大治四方則之夾
谷之會兵萊夷歸侵田折齊奸謀以重魯
於天下徒道大春秋莫能究其用而其門
人高第各能以其道用之諸侯若子路用
蒲而治言游用武城而治不齊用單父而
治顔淵雖不仕而深潜純粹王佐之才已
具有其德而無其用者吾未之前聞也夫
良劒昆吾冶之越砥礪之清水淬之鵜鶘
膏之則必割矣否則必惡劒也騏驥直中
punctuated: 之信也而愚，子羔之孝也而愚，孟公綽優於趙、魏老，不可以爲滕、薛大夫，鮑叔牙忠信廉潔，而不可以託國。當彼所謂德者，顓固曲方之行耳。今四子而古之德也，有不可以大受者乎？是故有伊尹、傅說之德，則必能阿衡商業，舟楫大川；有周公之德，則必能勝殷遏劉，朝委裘而致太平。孔子曰：「有德者必有言，仁者必有勇。」又曰：「我戰則克，祭則受福。」故仕魯三月，男女別于途，道不拾遺，市不預價，魯國大治，四方則之。夾谷之會，兵萊夷，歸侵田，折齊奸謀，以重魯於天下。徒道大，春秋莫能究其用，而其門人高第各能以其道用之諸侯。若子路用蒲而治，言游用武城而治，不齊用單父而治；顔淵雖不仕，而深潜純粹，王佐之才已具。有其德而無其用者，吾未之前聞也。夫良劒，昆吾冶之，越砥礪之，清水淬之，鵜鶘膏之，則必割矣，否則必惡劒也。騏驥，直中…
translation_en: …trustworthiness was foolish; Zigao's 子羔 filial piety was foolish; Meng Gongchuo 孟公綽 was more than adequate to serve as a household steward of the Zhao 趙 or Wei 魏 clans, yet unfit to be a grand master of the states of Teng 滕 or Xue 薛; and Bao Shuya 鮑叔牙 was loyal, trustworthy, and incorruptible, yet one could not entrust the state to him. What passed as "virtue" in their cases was merely obstinate, narrow-minded conduct. If these four men had truly possessed the virtue of the ancients, how could they have been incapable of assuming great responsibilities? Therefore, if one possesses the virtue of Yi Yin 伊尹 and Fu Yue 傅說, one will surely be able to serve as mainstay to the enterprise of the Shang 商 and as boat and oars across the great river; if one possesses the virtue of the Duke of Zhou 周公, one will surely be able to conquer Yin 殷 and halt the slaughter, holding court with robes draped relaxedly while bringing about great peace. Confucius 孔子 said: "One who possesses virtue is sure to have worthy words; one who is humane is sure to have courage." He also said: "When I fight, I prevail; when I sacrifice, I receive blessings." Thus, when he held office in Lu 魯 for three months, men and women kept to separate sides of the road, lost items were not picked up on the highways, merchants in the marketplace did not inflate their prices, the state of Lu was brought to great order, and the four quarters took it as their model. At the meeting at Jiagu 夾谷, he repelled the Lai barbarians 萊夷 by force of arms, recovered the encroached lands, and thwarted the treacherous plots of Qi 齊, thereby giving Lu great weight across the empire. It was only because his Way was so vast that none in the Spring and Autumn period could fully exhaust his usefulness; yet his foremost disciples were each able to apply his Way in the service of the feudal lords. For instance, Zilu 子路 was employed in Pu 蒲 and brought it to order; Yan You 言游 was employed in Wucheng 武城 and brought it to order; Fuzi Buqi 宓不齊 [Buqi 不齊] was employed in Shanfu 單父 and brought it to order; and although Yan Yuan 顔淵 did not take office, in his deep immersion and pure refinement the talent of a kingly aide was already complete. That someone could possess such virtue and yet lack its practical application is something I have never heard of before. Now, as for a fine sword: if it is smelted at Kunwu 昆吾, honed on a whetstone of Yue 越, tempered in clear water, and greased with pelican fat, it will surely cut; otherwise, it must be an inferior sword. As for a thoroughbred steed (Qiji 騏驥), if its straight movement hits…

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
繩曲中鉤方中矩圓中規則必馳矣否則
必駑馬也相士者蓋亦若是矣而世之人
往往失之則何以故聲實不辨一好惡偏
私二毀譽亂眞三古之善相馬者寒風氏
相口齒麻朝相頰子女厲相目衞忌相髭
許鄙相臋投伐褐相胸脅管青相臏膓陳
悲相股脚秦牙相前贊君相後非一徵也
廼九方歅又得之牝牡驪黃之外矣夫士
亦然固不可以淺見一方知也是故秉禮
===
勅躬近乎傲正靜遠俗近乎迂內辨少言
近乎愚虛體謙遜近乎卑持法不骯近乎
武健是非不回近乎訐直薄名寡交儉於
奔走周容近乎疏士之不耦於俗者大都
若此矣剽輕儇捷者似敏嘽咺多偶者似
信炙𨍏滑稽者似智乘權隻立者似剛窒
拗自是者似執俶詭跅弛者似豪脫毛察
瑣委者似精明嫗煦悅人者似和愛虛譚
隱借者似高邈敝衣冠設辭讓者似乎廉
punctuated: 繩，曲中鉤，方中矩，圓中規，則必馳矣，否則必駑馬也。相士者蓋亦若是矣，而世之人往往失之，則何以故？聲實不辨一，好惡偏私二，毀譽亂眞三。古之善相馬者，寒風氏相口齒，麻朝相頰，子女厲相目，衞忌相髭，許鄙相臋，投伐褐相胸脅，管青相臏膓，陳悲相股脚，秦牙相前，贊君相後，非一徵也；廼九方歅又得之牝牡驪黃之外矣。夫士亦然，固不可以淺見一方知也。是故秉禮勅躬，近乎傲；正靜遠俗，近乎迂；內辨少言，近乎愚；虛體謙遜，近乎卑；持法不骯，近乎武健；是非不回，近乎訐直；薄名寡交，儉於奔走周容，近乎疏。士之不耦於俗者，大都若此矣。剽輕儇捷者似敏，嘽咺多偶者似信，炙𨍏滑稽者似智，乘權隻立者似剛，窒拗自是者似執，俶詭跅弛者似豪，脫毛察瑣委者似精明，嫗煦悅人者似和愛，虛譚隱借者似高邈，敝衣冠、設辭讓者似乎廉
translation_en: … [when running] straight it conforms to the marking line, when turning it conforms to the hook, when squaring off it conforms to the carpenter's square, and when circling it conforms to the compass, then it will surely gallop swiftly; otherwise, it must be an inferior horse. Judging scholars is presumably just like this, yet people in the world often get it wrong—for what reason? First, reputation and reality are not distinguished; second, likes and dislikes are biased and selfish; third, slander and praise confound the truth. Among those of antiquity skilled at judging horses, Master Hanfeng 寒風氏 examined the mouth and teeth, Ma Chao 麻朝 examined the cheeks, Zinyu Li 子女厲 examined the eyes, Wei Ji 衞忌 examined the whiskers, Xu Bi 許鄙 examined the rump, Tou Fahe 投伐褐 examined the chest and flanks, Guan Qing 管青 examined the kneecaps and bowels [?], Chen Bei 陳悲 examined the thighs and legs, Qin Ya 秦牙 examined the forequarters, and Zanjun 贊君 examined the hindquarters—they did not rely on a single sign; whereas Jiufang Yin 九方歅 grasped it altogether beyond whether the horse was mare or stallion, black or yellow. Now it is the same with scholars: assuredly they cannot be known through shallow views or a single aspect. Therefore, holding fast to ritual and disciplining oneself comes close to arrogance; being upright, calm, and aloof from the vulgar comes close to pedantry; having inner discernment while speaking little comes close to stupidity; keeping oneself empty and modest comes close to servility; upholding the law without bending [?] comes close to harsh aggressiveness; not wavering over right and wrong comes close to abrasive bluntness; caring little for fame, having few associates, and being sparing in rushing about to curry favor comes close to alienation. Scholars who do not conform to the vulgar world are for the most part like this. On the other hand, those who are frivolous, nimble, and glib resemble the quick-witted; those who are effusive and have many companions [?] resemble the trustworthy; those who are slick as a greased axle and smooth-talking resemble the wise; those who ride on power and stand alone resemble the resolute; those who are obstinate and self-righteous resemble the steadfast; those who are eccentric and unrestrained resemble the heroic; those who split hairs and scrutinize trivialities resemble the astute; those who coddle and please others resemble the harmonious and loving; those who engage in empty talk and veiled pretexts [?] resemble the lofty and remote; and those who wear tattered caps and robes and put on displays of polite refusal seem to be of pure…

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
約士之鮮實行者大都若此矣語曰相馬
失之肥相劒失之室是以仲尼重信於子
羽卞和垂泣於荆璞故形實不可不辨也
人固難知知人亦不易有味乎其言之也
世晩士不聞道褊中陰賊難以勝數有識
鑒卑闇本不足以知之者有好惡偏頗乖
其所知者有明知之而倒植臧否者又常
好其從諛而和已者不好其介特而異已
者好其柔媚而下已者不好其莊競而抗
===
已者好其綢繆而親已者不好其疏節而
遠已者見人之長則忌之從而掎摘之矣
聞人譽人之善則妬之隨而巧詆之矣好
惡若此可不爲太息乎於是毁譽紛淫不
可方物其譽人也刓方比周而當之允達
之士譎譑姺㜺而當之亮直之士響應單
至而當之連敏之士伺色窺指而當之警
穎之士纍尾結繩而當之該通之士其毁
人也方正醜汙而少之曰乖盭深堅不奪
punctuated: 約。士之鮮實行者，大都若此矣。語曰：「相馬失之肥，相劒失之室。」是以仲尼重信於子羽，卞和垂泣於荆璞。故形實不可不辨也。人固難知，知人亦不易，有味乎其言之也！世晩，士不聞道，褊中陰賊，難以勝數。有識鑒卑闇，本不足以知之者；有好惡偏頗，乖其所知者；有明知之，而倒植臧否者。又常好其從諛而和已者，不好其介特而異已者；好其柔媚而下已者，不好其莊競而抗已者；好其綢繆而親已者，不好其疏節而遠已者。見人之長則忌之，從而掎摘之矣；聞人譽人之善則妬之，隨而巧詆之矣。好惡若此，可不爲太息乎！於是毁譽紛淫，不可方物。其譽人也，刓方比周，而當之允達之士；譎譑姺㜺，而當之亮直之士；響應單至，而當之連敏之士；伺色窺指，而當之警穎之士；纍尾結繩，而當之該通之士。其毁人也，方正醜汙，而少之曰乖盭；深堅不奪，
translation_en:
… and frugal. Those scholars who lack substantive conduct are for the most part like this. As the saying goes: "In judging horses, one errs by looking at their fatness; in judging swords, one errs by looking at their scabbards." For this reason, Zhongni (Confucius) reconsidered his trust in Ziyu (Tantai Mieming 澹臺滅明), and Bian He 卞和 shed tears over the uncut jade of Jing. Therefore, outward appearance and inner reality must be distinguished. People are inherently difficult to know, and knowing people is likewise not easy—how meaningful are those words!

In a degenerate age, scholars do not hear the Way; those who are narrow-minded and secretly malicious are too numerous to count. There are those whose discernment is low and benighted, who are fundamentally incapable of knowing others; there are those whose likes and dislikes are biased, perverting what they do know; and there are those who clearly know someone, yet invert their judgment of good and bad. Moreover, they constantly favor those who flatter and echo them, and dislike those who stand independent and differ from them; they favor those who are compliant, obsequious, and deferential to them, and dislike those who are dignified, unyielding, and stand up to them; they favor those who cultivate close ties and cleave to them, and dislike those who are negligent of social niceties and keep their distance from them. When they see others' strengths, they resent them, and proceed to find fault and pick at them; when they hear someone praising others' goodness, they are jealous of them, and forthwith artfully slander them. When likes and dislikes are such as this, how can one not heave a deep sigh?

Consequently, slander and praise become confused and excessive, beyond all measure or distinction. When they praise people: those who round off their squareness and form partisan cliques, they regard as sincere and通達 [accomplished] scholars; those who are deceitful, crafty, and sharply contentious [? 姺㜺], they regard as upright and straightforward scholars; those who answer like an echo and come running at a single call, they regard as nimble and swift-minded scholars; those who watch countenances and spy out intentions, they regard as alert and acute scholars; those who trail behind and tie knots [in collusion], they regard as comprehensive and learned scholars. When they slander people: those who are square, upright, and loathe corruption, they belittle as perverse and refractory; those who are deeply steadfast and cannot be swayed from their resolve, …

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
而少之曰愚戇靖恭伏職而少之曰巽懦
欲傅人以椎鈍不曰椎鈍而譽之曰天性
悃厚欲傅人以鷙擊不曰鷙擊而譽之曰
峭厲善理欲傅人以呰窳不曰呰窳而曰
政尚寬平昔之傾人者毀之今之傾人者
譽之矣昔之毀人者構誣之今之毀人者
嘆息之矣昔也謂貞女爲淫今也以桑中
而詆貞女矣昔也謂鏌釾爲鈍今也以鉛
刀而咲鏌釾矣毀譽若此安得無亂眞乎
===
夫迷謬好惡者逆蘭茝而悅讎糜者也錯
糅毀譽者刻畫無鹽而點毛嬙者也信耳
者羣犬吠聲者也信目者見攫煤飯者也
重信耳目者膽胥之疑耳目人終無巳者
也惑於形似者燕石爲玉之類也惑於聲
似者鼠璞爲璞之類也失於似而因疑其
眞者黎丘丈人之智懲於祟而失其子者
也是數者皆士之害也而好惡爲尤好惡
正而後可與言辨材之道焉夫九方歅之
punctuated:
而少之曰愚戇，靖恭伏職而少之曰巽懦。欲傅人以椎鈍，不曰椎鈍，而譽之曰天性悃厚；欲傅人以鷙擊，不曰鷙擊，而譽之曰峭厲善理；欲傅人以呰窳，不曰呰窳，而曰政尚寬平。昔之傾人者毀之，今之傾人者譽之矣；昔之毀人者構誣之，今之毀人者嘆息之矣；昔也謂貞女爲淫，今也以桑中而詆貞女矣；昔也謂鏌釾爲鈍，今也以鉛刀而咲鏌釾矣。毀譽若此，安得無亂眞乎？
夫迷謬好惡者，逆蘭茝而悅讎糜者也；錯糅毀譽者，刻畫無鹽而點毛嬙者也；信耳者，羣犬吠聲者也；信目者，見攫煤飯者也；重信耳目者，膽胥之疑耳目人終無巳者也；惑於形似者，燕石爲玉之類也；惑於聲似者，鼠璞爲璞之類也；失於似而因疑其眞者，黎丘丈人之智，懲於祟而失其子者也。是數者，皆士之害也，而好惡爲尤。好惡正，而後可與言辨材之道焉。夫九方歅之
translation_en:
…they belittle them as foolish and obtuse; those who quietly and respectfully fulfill their duties they belittle as timid and weak. When they wish to pin the label of dullness on someone, they do not call him dull, but praise him as having an innately sincere and simple nature; when they wish to pin the label of ruthless harshness on someone, they do not call him ruthlessly harsh, but praise him as being sternly decisive and skilled in administration; when they wish to pin the label of indolence and negligence on someone, they do not call him indolent and negligent, but say his governance values leniency and calm. In the past, those who sought to bring others down slandered them; today, those who seek to bring others down praise them. In the past, those who slandered others fabricated false charges against them; today, those who slander others sigh over them in feigned regret. In the past, they called a chaste woman licentious; today, they use the licentious airs of "Amidst the Mulberries" (Sangzhong) to disparage a chaste woman. In the past, they called the legendary Moye sword blunt; today, they use a lead knife to laugh at the Moye sword. When slander and praise are like this, how can the truth not be confounded?

Now, those whose likes and dislikes are deluded and perverse are like people who are repelled by fragrant orchids and angelica yet delight in foul dregs [?]. Those who jumble together slander and praise are like people who prettify the ugly Wuyan while sullying the beautiful Mao Qiang. Those who trust only their ears are like a pack of dogs barking at a sound; those who trust only their eyes are like Confucius seeing Yan Hui snatching up soot-stained rice. Those who overly trust their “ears and eyes” [informants] are like Dan Xu [?], whose suspicions through informants never ceased. Those who are deceived by outward resemblance are like the man who mistook a stone from Yan for jade; those who are deceived by verbal similarity are like the merchant who mistook an unskinned rat ("rat-in-the-rough") for uncut jade ("jade-in-the-rough"). Those who are misled by a semblance and consequently doubt the genuine article are like the old man of Liqiu, whose supposed cleverness, made wary by a shape-shifting demon, caused him to kill his own son. All several of these are harmful to scholars, and biased likes and dislikes are the worst among them. Only when likes and dislikes are rectified can one speak of the way of discerning talent. That Jiufang Yin…

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
不失馬也豈獨其技殊絕哉彼無好惡於
馬以亂其視也故鑑之所貴不在乎明而
在乎空空則妍醜隨形而明矣衡之所貴
不在於星而在於權以意行權則低昂失
而星廢矣是以嫫女不怨鑑而貪夫服於
衡嗚呼人皆正大不私怨惡則賢不肖白
而人心服士不下蔽賢才輻湊而
聖君賢臣設燎捉髮之心庶幾哉無負矣執事
所謂共由大道者意在斯乎
===
第四問
同考試官訓導王批纘序譜牒以存古宗法意
遠矣子能縷悉之可謂多聞
考試官學正陳批譜家互持異說此作折衷
得其要領
考試官學正王批博辨閎肆而具道本根詳
核有體
譜牒者其古道之遺乎其起於古道之廢
punctuated:
不失馬也，豈獨其技殊絕哉？彼無好惡於馬以亂其視也。故鑑之所貴，不在乎明而在乎空，空則妍醜隨形而明矣；衡之所貴，不在於星而在於權，以意行權，則低昂失而星廢矣。是以嫫女不怨鑑，而貪夫服於衡。嗚呼！人皆正大，不私怨惡，則賢不肖白而人心服，士不下蔽，賢才輻湊，而聖君賢臣設燎捉髮之心，庶幾哉無負矣！執事所謂共由大道者，意在斯乎？

第四問
同考試官訓導王批：纘序譜牒以存古宗法，意遠矣。子能縷悉之，可謂多聞。
考試官學正陳批：譜家互持異說，此作折衷，得其要領。
考試官學正王批：博辨閎肆，而具道本根，詳核有體。

譜牒者，其古道之遺乎？其起於古道之廢
translation_en:
…never failed in judging a horse—was it merely because his skill was extraordinarily supreme? It was because he harbored no personal likes or dislikes toward horses to cloud his vision. Therefore, what is valued in a mirror lies not in its brightness, but in its emptiness; when it is empty, beauty and ugliness are clearly reflected according to their forms. What is valued in a balance scale lies not in the markings on the beam, but in the sliding weight; if one moves the weight according to personal whim, then high and low lose their measure and the markings become useless. Thus, an ugly woman like Mo Mu does not resent the mirror, and a greedy man submits to the scale. Alas! If everyone is upright and magnanimous, without private resentments or aversions, then the worthy and the unworthy will be clearly distinguished and people's hearts will submit; scholars will not be obscured below, worthy talents will converge like spokes at a hub, and the earnest heart of the sage ruler and worthy ministers—setting out torches at dawn to receive guests and grasping their wet hair mid-wash to welcome talent—will nearly not have been in vain! Is this not the meaning of what Your Excellency calls the Great Way that all should follow?

Fourth Question

Comment by Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Wang: Compiling genealogies in order to preserve the ancient lineage system is a far-reaching idea. That you are able to recount them in full detail shows that you may be called well-informed.

Comment by Examiner and Subprefectural Director of Studies Chen: Genealogists hold mutually conflicting views; this essay strikes a balanced judgment and grasps the essential points.

Comment by Examiner and Subprefectural Director of Studies Wang: Broadly argued, expansive and unrestrained, yet it fully articulates the fundamental roots; it is detailed, verified, and well-structured.

Are genealogical records a remnant of the ancient Way? Or did they arise from the decline of the ancient Way…

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
乎古有之大宗者收族者也譜牒者其
大宗之遺乎雖然有大宗則無譜牒故
譜牒者起於大宗之廢也古者因族而
立之宗因宗而示之統握其權於上則
聯屬之勢似渙而實合明其制於下則
綱維之法似疎而實詳夫是可以勸忠
可以作孝可以收族亦可以廣仁敎化
行而廉耻重愛敬漸而德讓流職此故
也晚近世宗法廢而天下無世家歷世
===
滋蔓子孫至不知先人名行長老倒植
視宗黨乃如路人異時殊勢陵敎隋義賢
者傷之於是官有簿狀以紀民之盛衰家
有譜系以紀族之分合保姓鳩族扶義翼
敎使民相親長敦本不忘蓋有宗法之遺
焉且姓氏之學譚非易易也雖司馬遷劉
知幾博聞良史猶以周公爲姬旦文王爲
姬伯尚以姬姜嬴姒爲女婦之稱而況於
愚生乎然甞聞之矣三代之前姓氏分爲
punctuated:
乎？古有之：「大宗者，收族者也。」譜牒者，其大宗之遺乎！雖然，有大宗則無譜牒，故譜牒者，起於大宗之廢也。古者因族而立之宗，因宗而示之統。握其權於上，則聯屬之勢似渙而實合；明其制於下，則綱維之法似疎而實詳。夫是可以勸忠，可以作孝，可以收族，亦可以廣仁。敎化行而廉耻重，愛敬漸而德讓流，職此故也。晚近世宗法廢而天下無世家，歷世滋蔓，子孫至不知先人名行，長老倒植，視宗黨乃如路人，異時殊勢，陵敎隋義，賢者傷之。於是官有簿狀以紀民之盛衰，家有譜系以紀族之分合，保姓鳩族，扶義翼敎，使民相親長，敦本不忘，蓋有宗法之遺焉。

且姓氏之學，譚非易易也。雖司馬遷、劉知幾博聞良史，猶以周公爲姬旦、文王爲姬伯，尚以姬、姜、嬴、姒爲女婦之稱，而況於愚生乎？然甞聞之矣：三代之前，姓氏分爲
translation_en:
… [or did they arise from the decay of the ancient Way]? There is an ancient saying: "The great lineage (dazong) is that which gathers the kin together." Genealogical registers—are they not the remnant of the great lineage! Even so, when the great lineage existed, there were no genealogical registers; thus, genealogical registers arose from the decay of the great lineage. In antiquity, on the basis of the kin group, a lineage was established for them; on the basis of the lineage, a line of succession was demonstrated to them. When authority over it was held above, the dynamic of their cohesion seemed dispersed yet was in reality united; when its institutions were made clear below, the framework of its regulations seemed loose yet was in reality detailed. Thus, by this means one could encourage loyalty, foster filial piety, gather the kin together, and also broaden benevolence. That moral transformation was carried out and a sense of integrity and shame was valued, and that love and respect gradually took hold while virtuous deference spread—all was due to this. In more recent ages, the patriarchal lineage system (zongfa) fell into disuse, and the empire had no hereditary houses. As generations passed and branches multiplied, descendants reached the point of not knowing the names and conduct of their forebears; seniority was inverted, and people regarded their own lineage members and kinsmen just like strangers on the road. As times changed and circumstances differed, moral teaching was transgressed and righteousness grew lax [Reading 隋 as 惰]. Worthy men grieved over this. Thereupon, the government had official registers of status (bozhuang) to record the rise and decline of the people, and families had genealogical tables (puxi) to record the branching and uniting of the kin—preserving surnames and assembling clans, upholding righteousness and supporting moral teaching, causing the people to be affectionate toward one another and respect their elders, and to esteem their roots without forgetting. In this there was indeed something of the remnant of the lineage system.

Moreover, the study of ancestral surnames (xing) and clan names (shi) is by no means an easy matter to discuss. Even Sima Qian 司馬遷 and Liu Zhiji 劉知幾, who were broadly learned and fine historians, still referred to the Duke of Zhou 周公 as Ji Dan 姬旦 and King Wen 文王 as Ji Bo 姬伯, and still took Ji 姬, Jiang 姜, Ying 嬴, and Si 姒 to be designations exclusivos to women—how much more so for a foolish student like myself? Yet I have heard it said: before the Three Dynasties, surnames (xing) and clan names (shi) were divided into…

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
二三代之後姓氏混而爲一古者姓氏之
權出於上故族類易明後世姓氏之柄寄
於民故枝派難考善乎東萊呂氏之言曰
姓者統其祖考之所自出百世而不變者
也氏者別其子孫之所自分數世而一變
者也古者天子胙諸侯公卿大夫之土則
各命之氏諸侯公卿大夫士之家各按其
氏系以宗法行世祿之典其比閭州黨之
民不及以世祿者亦繇口受之業長子孫
===
於其土而太宰又以九兩之法繫之故其
族不散洽敘敦固而俗不漓有以也中世
以來諸侯公卿大夫士之世不及祿支離
分散枝蔓于中國又革命之際所當兵燹
戰陳與夫饑饉亡徙者不可勝數州郡之
間求如春秋世家者且不可得而况於古
者氏系所出乎此學士大夫所以歔欷嘆
息而譜所由作也漢司馬子長採世本世
系而作帝紀據周譜國語而作世家姓氏
punctuated: 二；三代之後，姓氏混而爲一。古者姓氏之權出於上，故族類易明；後世姓氏之柄寄於民，故枝派難考。善乎東萊呂氏之言曰：「姓者，統其祖考之所自出，百世而不變者也；氏者，別其子孫之所自分，數世而一變者也。」古者天子胙諸侯、公、卿、大夫之土，則各命之氏；諸侯、公、卿、大夫、士之家，各按其氏系，以宗法行世祿之典。其比、閭、州、黨之民，不及以世祿者，亦繇口受之業，長子孫於其土，而太宰又以九兩之法繫之。故其族不散，洽敘敦固，而俗不漓，有以也。中世以來，諸侯、公、卿、大夫、士之世不及祿，支離分散，枝蔓于中國；又革命之際，所當兵燹戰陳，與夫饑饉亡徙者，不可勝數。州郡之間，求如春秋世家者且不可得，而况於古者氏系所出乎？此學士大夫所以歔欷嘆息，而譜所由作也。漢司馬子長採《世本》世系而作《帝紀》，據《周譜》、《國語》而作《世家》，姓氏
translation_en: … two; after the Three Dynasties, surnames (xing) and clan names (shi) merged into one. In antiquity, the authority over surnames and clan names issued from above, so kindred and lineages were easy to clarify; in later ages, control over surnames and clan names rested with the common people, so branches and offshoots became difficult to trace. Well said are the words of Master Lü of Donglai (Lü Zuqian 呂祖謙): "The surname (xing) unites those who issue from the same remote ancestors and does not change for a hundred generations; the clan name (shi) distinguishes where descendants branch off from one another and changes once every few generations." In antiquity, when the Son of Heaven bestowed land upon feudal lords, dukes, ministers, and grand masters, he conferred a clan name upon each of them; the families of feudal lords, dukes, ministers, grand masters, and servicemen each followed their clan lineage to practice the institution of hereditary emoluments through the patriarchal clan law (zongfa). As for the commoners of the five-family neighborhoods (bi), twenty-five-family villages (lü), districts (zhou), and communities (dang) who did not attain hereditary emoluments, they too raised their sons and grandsons on their land through per-capita allotments of property, while the Grand Councilor (Taizai) bound them together with the law of the Nine Bonds (jiu liang). Therefore, there was good reason why their clans did not scatter, their harmony and order were solid and firm, and their customs did not degenerate. Since the middle ages, the descendants of feudal lords, dukes, ministers, grand masters, and servicemen have not received hereditary emoluments, becoming fragmented, scattered, and sprawling across the central states; moreover, during dynastic revolutions, those who suffered the ravages of war and battle, or who fled and migrated because of famine, were beyond count. Among the prefectures and commanderies, one cannot even find hereditary houses like those of the Spring and Autumn period, let alone trace the ancient origins of clan lineages! This is why scholar-officials sigh and lament, and why genealogies came to be compiled. In the Han dynasty, Sima Zichang (Sima Qian 司馬遷) gathered the genealogical lineages from the Book of Origins (Shiben 世本) to compose the "Basic Annals of the Emperors" (Diji), and relied on the Zhou Genealogies (Zhoupu 周譜) and Discourses of the States (Guoyu 國語) to compose the "Hereditary Houses" (Shijia), whereby the … of surnames and clan names…

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
之源始著晉魏而降區區綜核百氏以門
第官人雖卑姓雜譜皆藏有司迄於李唐
猶相崇重故應邵則有氏族篇王僧孺則
有百家譜徐勉之則有百官牒河南則有
官氏志諸儒則有氏族志栁冲則有百姓
系錄路淳則有衣冠譜韋述則有開元譜
栁方則有永泰譜栁璨則有韻略張九齡
則有韻譜非不綦然列也然槩之有三種
焉論字者以偏旁為主是字書之工也論
===
聲者以四聲為主是韻聲之資也論地望
者以貴賤為主是升沈之恒也其弊也尚
婚婭者先外族而後本宗尚人物者進庶
孽而退嫡長尚冠冕者略伉儷而慕榮華
尚貴戚者狥勢利而忘禮教人無反本之
思而族鮮敦睦之道尚安望其乆安而長
治也哉嗚呼譜牒之盛也晉魏氏之失也
非自晉魏氏始也其始於宗法之亡乎至
於今譜又不存學士大夫莫知所自而仁
punctuated: 之源始著。晉魏而降，區區綜核百氏，以門第官人，雖卑姓雜譜皆藏有司，迄於李唐，猶相崇重。故應邵則有《氏族篇》，王僧孺則有《百家譜》，徐勉之則有《百官牒》，河南則有《官氏志》，諸儒則有《氏族志》，栁冲則有《百姓系錄》，路淳則有《衣冠譜》，韋述則有《開元譜》，栁方則有《永泰譜》，栁璨則有《韻略》，張九齡則有《韻譜》，非不綦然列也。然槩之有三種焉：論字者以偏旁為主，是字書之工也；論聲者以四聲為主，是韻聲之資也；論地望者以貴賤為主，是升沈之恒也。其弊也，尚婚婭者先外族而後本宗，尚人物者進庶孽而退嫡長，尚冠冕者略伉儷而慕榮華，尚貴戚者狥勢利而忘禮教。人無反本之思，而族鮮敦睦之道，尚安望其乆安而長治也哉！嗚呼！譜牒之盛也，晉魏氏之失也。非自晉魏氏始也，其始於宗法之亡乎？至於今，譜又不存，學士大夫莫知所自，而仁
translation_en: …the origins of [surnames and clans] first became clear. From the Wei and Jin dynasties onward, people busied themselves with verifying and collating the hundred clans, appointing men to office on the basis of family status. Even the miscellaneous genealogies of lowly surnames were all stored with the authorities, and down to the Tang dynasty of the Li house, they were still mutually revered and valued. Thus Ying Shao had the Treatise on Clans and Lineages (Shizu pian), Wang Sengru had the Genealogies of the Hundred Families (Baijia pu), Xu Mianzhi [Xu Mian] had the Registers of the Hundred Officials (Baiguan die), Henan [YuanCha/Northern Wei] had the Treatise on Official Clans (Guanshi zhi), the various scholars had the Treatise on Clans and Lineages (Shizu zhi), Liu Chong had the Lineage Records of the Hundred Surnames (Baixing xilu), Lu Chun [Lu Jingchun] had the Genealogies of Officialdom (Yiguan pu), Wei Shu had the Kaiyuan Genealogies (Kaiyuan pu), Liu Fang had the Yongtai Genealogies (Yongtai pu), Liu Can had the Rhyming Compendium (Yunlüe), and Zhang Jiuling had the Rhymed Genealogies (Yunpu)—it is not that they were not arrayed in intricate order! Yet broadly speaking, they fall into three categories: those that arrange by character take the radical as primary, which is the craft of character dictionaries; those that arrange by sound take the four tones as primary, which is an aid to rhyme and phonology; and those that arrange by choronymic prestige take noble and base status as primary, which reflects the vicissitudes of rise and fall. As for their abuses: those who prize marriage alliances put affinal relatives first and their own patrilineal clan last; those who prize individual talent promote concubines' sons and demote the eldest legitimate son; those who prize official caps and robes slight proper matrimonial matches and covet glory and splendor; and those who prize noble relatives pursue power and profit while forgetting ritual teaching. People lack the thought of returning to their roots, and clans rarely possess the way of cordial harmony—how then can one still hope for enduring peace and lasting order? Alas! The flourishing of genealogical registers was the failing of the Wei and Jin; yet it did not begin with the Wei and Jin—did it not begin with the demise of the patriarchal clan system (zongfa)? Coming down to the present day, genealogies in turn no longer survive; scholars and officials do not know whence they came, and the [hearts of] benevolent…

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
人孝子之心茫乎無所寄於是扼腕而嘆
抵掌而譚以求復宗法而宗卒不可立其
亦未明於古今之變乎夫宗法不可行於
今者有三封建不復舉矣學校不復修矣
井田不復制矣其不可行者勢也古者諸
侯世其國別子世大夫故宗立而族人莫
不聽焉今之大夫起於白屋非有尺寸之
籍也載符而出受代而旋非有定位可以
長子孫也故紈袴之後同於隸廝怙惡之
===
踪不齒族黨其身之不自淑而又皇恤其
他此其不可行者一也書曰世祿之家鮮
克由禮故師氏正其行保氏授其文而又
司過議其宥故其教易尊而宗可久也漢
承秦制破滅世家二千石皆以鋤治彊宗
豪右爲政於是景屈諸田之族且下隸編
氓矣況望其纘世業而明禮教哉此其不
可行者二也三代之制各有夫田分業定
而衣食足然後民依於宗而不麗於法令
punctuated: 人孝子之心，茫乎無所寄。於是扼腕而嘆，抵掌而譚，以求復宗法，而宗卒不可立，其亦未明於古今之變乎！夫宗法不可行於今者有三：封建不復舉矣，學校不復修矣，井田不復制矣；其不可行者，勢也。古者諸侯世其國，別子世大夫，故宗立而族人莫不聽焉。今之大夫起於白屋，非有尺寸之籍也；載符而出，受代而旋，非有定位可以長子孫也。故紈袴之後，同於隸廝；怙惡之踪，不齒族黨。其身之不自淑，而又皇恤其他？此其不可行者一也。《書》曰：「世祿之家，鮮克由禮。」故師氏正其行，保氏授其文，而又司過議其宥，故其教易尊而宗可久也。漢承秦制，破滅世家，二千石皆以鋤治彊宗豪右爲政，於是景、屈、諸田之族，且下隸編氓矣，況望其纘世業而明禮教哉？此其不可行者二也。三代之制，各有夫田，分業定而衣食足，然後民依於宗而不麗於法。今
translation_en:
…the hearts of humane men and filial sons are left bewildered, with nothing to rely upon. Thereupon they wring their hands and sigh, clap their palms and discourse at length, seeking to restore the descent-line system (zongfa); yet in the end the descent-line cannot be established. Is this not because they have failed to understand the changes between antiquity and the present!

There are three reasons why the descent-line system cannot be practiced today: enfeoffment (fengjian) is no longer instituted, the ancient schools are no longer maintained, and the well-field system (jingtian) is no longer established. That it cannot be practiced is a matter of historical circumstance.

In antiquity, the feudal lords held their states by hereditary succession, and their secondary sons held the rank of Grand Master (dafu) by hereditary succession; therefore, once the descent-line was established, none among the kinsmen failed to obey it. Today’s Grand Masters rise from humble thatched cottages, possessing not an inch of hereditary status; they carry their credentials when going out to take office and return home when replaced, having no fixed position by which to preside over their sons and grandsons. Thus, the descendants of silk-trousered scions become no different from menials and servants, and the conduct of those who persist in wrongdoing leaves them despised by their own clansmen and neighbors. When they cannot even cultivate virtue in their own persons, how could they have leisure to care for others? This is the first reason it cannot be practiced.

The Book of Documents (Shu) says: “Families of hereditary emolument rarely abide by ritual propriety.” Therefore, in antiquity, the Master of Instruction (shishi) rectified their conduct, the Protector (baoshi) taught them cultural refinement, and the Official in Charge of Offenses (siguo) deliberated on pardons for them; thus their teaching was easily revered and the descent-line could endure. When the Han succeeded to the institutions of the Qin, it broke and destroyed the hereditary houses, and the Two-Thousand-Bushel Officials (erqianshi, i.e., Commandery Governors) all made the eradication of powerful clans and local magnates the core of their governance. Thereupon, such clans as the Jing, the Qu, and the various branches of the Tian were reduced to the status of registered commoners—how much less could one hope for them to carry on hereditary callings and clarify ritual teaching? This is the second reason it cannot be practiced.

Under the institutions of the Three Dynasties, each household had its allotment of land; once their allotted livelihoods were settled and food and clothing were sufficient, the people relied upon their descent-line and did not fall foul of the laws. Today…

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
者民無常業士鮮固志卽使士師議刑憲
人執法尚不能使遊食者外無異謀乃欲
假服制聯親屬抗宗法以復古道豈不謬
哉此其不可行者三也然則有志反本者
將聽其宗之離散而不屬乎抑亦外譜牒
而必復古大宗小宗之舊乎夫離散則有
所不忍矣泥古則有所不可矣惟於重譜
之中寓所以立宗之意焉可耳宋世言宗
譜者二家曰廬陵歐陽氏曰眉山蘇氏二
===
家之法厥各不同歐陽氏則世經人緯取
法於史氏之年表蘇氏則系聯派屬如禮
家所謂宗圖者及論所爲同則皆使人重
其本之所自出有尊尊之義焉各詳其支
之所由分有親親之道焉其法具在可攷
鏡也愚以謂民間支派悠邈莫可究詰者
不必强爲之附而諸所指覿可以譜牒行
者俾之族各爲譜譜各有表表各有圖上
自始祖下及子孫各以類系屬不相紊亂
punctuated:
者民無常業，士鮮固志，卽使士師議刑、憲人執法，尚不能使遊食者外無異謀，乃欲假服制、聯親屬、抗宗法以復古道，豈不謬哉？此其不可行者三也。
然則有志反本者，將聽其宗之離散而不屬乎？抑亦外譜牒而必復古大宗、小宗之舊乎？夫離散則有所不忍矣，泥古則有所不可矣，惟於重譜之中，寓所以立宗之意焉可耳。宋世言宗譜者二家：曰廬陵歐陽氏，曰眉山蘇氏。二家之法，厥各不同。歐陽氏則世經人緯，取法於史氏之年表；蘇氏則系聯派屬，如禮家所謂宗圖者。及論所爲同，則皆使人重其本之所自出，有尊尊之義焉；各詳其支之所由分，有親親之道焉。其法具在，可攷鏡也。
愚以謂民間支派悠邈、莫可究詰者，不必强爲之附；而諸所指覿、可以譜牒行者，俾之族各爲譜，譜各有表，表各有圖，上自始祖，下及子孫，各以類系屬，不相紊亂，
translation_en:
…[Now] the common people have no constant livelihood, and scholars rarely have steadfast resolve. Even if the Judicial Officers deliberate on punishments and the Censors enforce the laws, they still cannot keep idle consumers from harboring seditious schemes outside; yet should one wish to rely on mourning grades, bind together kinsmen, and elevate the descent-line system (zongfa) in order to restore the ancient way—how could that not be absurd? This is the third reason it cannot be practiced.

Well then, should those who aspire to return to the root simply allow their lineages to scatter and remain unconnected? Or should they disregard genealogical registers and insist upon restoring the old system of the ancient Great Lineage and Lesser Lineages? Now, to let them scatter is something one cannot bear, yet to cling rigidly to antiquity is something that cannot be done. Only by lodging the underlying principle of establishing the lineage within the emphasis on genealogies can it work. In the Song dynasty, there were two schools that spoke of clan genealogies: one called the Ouyang clan of Luling (Ouyang Xiu 歐陽修), and one called the Su clan of Meishan (Su Xun 蘇洵). The methods of the two schools were each different. The Ouyang clan used generations as the warp and individuals as the woof, taking its model from the chronological tables of the historians; the Su clan linked lines of descent and connected branches, like what ritualists call a lineage chart. Yet when we discuss what they had in common, both caused men to value the root from which they sprang, embodying the principle of honoring the honorable; and each detailed how its branches divided, embodying the way of loving one's kin. Their methods are preserved in full and can be examined as a mirror.

In my humble opinion, among the common people, where branch lines are remote and distant and cannot be thoroughly traced, one need not forcibly attach them together. But for all those whose relationships can be pointed out and witnessed [? 指覿], where genealogical registers can be put into practice, let each clan compile a genealogy, each genealogy have tables, and each table have charts. From the founding ancestor above down to the sons and grandsons below, let each be connected according to its category without confusion or disorder,…

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
略如二氏之制仍擇族之長且賢者司之
凡歳時伏臘朔望之旦無少長悉詣祠牒
者相敎以孝相率以友相勸以義相賙以
財諸不率者譙讓之斥不與齒則雖未嘗
強天下之勢以立之宗而宗法亦未嘗不
寓由是尊尊則人知有祖而分自明故曰
可以勸忠親親則人知有宗而恩愈篤故
曰可以作孝忠孝咸備故曰可以鳩族可
以廣仁焉嗚呼世道陵夷民窮而散編戶
===
之甿堇堇治其家人生產以爲是固慮足
仁義之譚乆遠之事里巷所詘卽語之未
遑也此其風非得世家大族薦紳先生儼
然爲齊民倡導安可幾乎夫日月星辰無
情也而皆宗於天百穀草木無情也而皆
宗於土別生分類無窮也而皆宗於祖宗
之義大矣哉然其權統於天子而其制成
於世臣此哲王所以達天親之本藎臣所
以明人道之懿而置天下於雍煕敦睦以
punctuated: 略如二氏之制。仍擇族之長且賢者司之，凡歳時伏臘、朔望之旦，無少長悉詣祠，牒者相敎以孝，相率以友，相勸以義，相賙以財。諸不率者譙讓之，斥不與齒。則雖未嘗強天下之勢以立之宗，而宗法亦未嘗不寓。由是尊尊，則人知有祖而分自明，故曰可以勸忠；親親，則人知有宗而恩愈篤，故曰可以作孝。忠孝咸備，故曰可以鳩族，可以廣仁焉。嗚呼！世道陵夷，民窮而散，編戶之甿，堇堇治其家人生產，以爲是固慮足；仁義之譚、乆遠之事，里巷所詘，卽語之未遑也。此其風，非得世家大族、薦紳先生儼然爲齊民倡導，安可幾乎？夫日月星辰無情也，而皆宗於天；百穀草木無情也，而皆宗於土；別生分類無窮也，而皆宗於祖。宗之義大矣哉！然其權統於天子，而其制成於世臣。此哲王所以達天親之本，藎臣所以明人道之懿，而置天下於雍煕敦睦，以
translation_en:
…roughly following the systems of the two masters [Ouyang and Su]. Furthermore, select an elder and worthy member of the lineage to take charge of it. On the mornings of seasonal festivals, summer and winter sacrifices, and the new and full moons, let everyone, young and old alike, go to the ancestral hall. Those recorded in the genealogy should teach one another filial piety, lead one another in fraternal affection, encourage one another in righteousness, and succor one another with wealth. Any who do not comply should be reprimanded and excluded from taking their place among the ranks of the kin. Thus, even without forcing the circumstances of the empire in order to establish major lineages, the principles of the lineage system will nonetheless be present within it. Through this, by honoring the honorable, people will know they have ancestors and status distinctions will naturally be clear; therefore it is said that this can encourage loyalty. By treating kin as kin, people will know they have a lineage and mutual affection will grow ever deeper; therefore it is said that this can foster filial piety. When loyalty and filial piety are both complete, it is said that one can gather the clan together and broaden benevolence.

Alas! Moral standards have declined, and the people are impoverished and scattered. The common folk of the registered households barely manage their own family livelihoods, considering that to be quite enough to worry about; talk of benevolence and righteousness and matters of long-term consequence are disparaged in the village lanes, and there is no leisure even to speak of them. How could such customs be hoped for unless hereditary houses, great clans, and gentry elders solemnly take the lead in guiding the common people? Now, the sun, moon, and stars have no consciousness, yet they all look to heaven as their source; the hundred grains, grasses, and trees have no consciousness, yet they all look to the earth as their source; people separated by birth and divided into kinds are无穷 [boundless in number], yet they all look to their ancestors as their source. Great indeed is the meaning of the ancestral lineage! Yet its authority is unified under the Son of Heaven, while its institution is brought to completion by hereditary ministers. This is how wise kings reach the root of heavenly kinship, and how loyal ministers clarify the excellence of the human way, placing the empire in a state of harmonious prosperity and cordiality, so as to…

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
庶幾復見三代之治者恃有此也可徒曰
宗法之廢也久矣遂聽其人之自相殘賊
也而莫為之所哉而非諸生所知也
第五問
同考試官教諭周批治在人不在法此根極之
論亟録之
考試官學正陳批留心世慮計有餘矣
考試官學正王批議畫有禆時事
===
法可變乎曰過然則不可變乎曰過夫法
變亦過不變亦過儳言而無所中有說乎
凡法久則必敝敝則民病病而不變過也
變之而不得其當當而不得其人行之無
益徒易之敝耳故曰變亦過也夫稷雖善
藝不能使禾冬生時也俞扁之方不必盡
用鄭衛之音不及輿諤宜也病變而藥不
變眾醫弗為矣人皆曰秦開阡陌罷侯置
守壞先王之法不知封建之法壞則不得
punctuated:
庶幾復見三代之治者，恃有此也。可徒曰「宗法之廢也久矣」，遂聽其人之自相殘賊也，而莫為之所哉？而非諸生所知也。
第五問
同考試官教諭周批：治在人不在法，此根極之論，亟録之。
考試官學正陳批：留心世慮，計有餘矣。
考試官學正王批：議畫有禆時事。
法可變乎？曰：過。然則不可變乎？曰：過。夫法變亦過，不變亦過，儳言而無所中，有說乎？凡法久則必敝，敝則民病，病而不變，過也；變之而不得其當，當而不得其人，行之無益，徒易之敝耳，故曰變亦過也。夫稷雖善藝，不能使禾冬生，時也；俞、扁之方，不必盡用，鄭、衛之音，不及輿諤，宜也。病變而藥不變，眾醫弗為矣。人皆曰：「秦開阡陌，罷侯置守，壞先王之法。」不知封建之法壞，則不得
translation_en:
… hope to see the governance of the Three Dynasties restored rests upon this. How could one merely say, "The lineage system has long since fallen into disuse," and consequently allow people to mutilate and harm one another without doing anything to put them in their proper place? Yet this is beyond what a Confucian student could know.

Fifth Question
Associate Examiner Instructor Zhou comments: Governance lies in men, not in laws. This is a fundamental and ultimate argument; record it at once.
Examiner Director of Studies Chen comments: Attentive to the concerns of the world; its plans are more than sufficient.
Examiner Director of Studies Wang comments: Its deliberations and plans are beneficial to current affairs.

Can laws be changed? One says: That is an error. Then can they not be changed? One says: That too is an error. Now if changing the laws is an error, and not changing them is also an error, is there an explanation for speaking so irregularly without hitting the mark? Whenever laws endure for a long time, they inevitably break down; when they break down, the people suffer. When the people suffer and the laws are not changed, that is an error. Yet if one changes them without achieving what is appropriate, or achieves what is appropriate without obtaining the right men, putting the changes into practice brings no benefit and merely replaces one abuse with another; therefore it is said that changing them is also an error. Though Hou Ji was skilled in husbandry, he could not make grain grow in winter—this is a matter of timeliness. The prescriptions of Yu Fu and Bian Que need not all be used, and the music of Zheng and Wei does not measure up to the chants of the multitude [?]—this is a matter of suitability. When an illness changes while the medicine remains unchanged, even ordinary physicians would not act thus. Everyone says, "Qin opened up the footpaths between fields, abolished the feudal lords and established commandery governors, thereby destroying the laws of the former kings." They do not realize that once the feudal system had broken down, one could not…

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
不盡為郡縣井田之法壞則不得不開阡
陌時與勢固然也秦之悖先王者固多此
未可以盡罪秦也今夫民情寒則欲火暑
則欲水燥則欲濕濕則欲燥寒暑燥濕相
反其於利民同也夫變法者亦以利民耳
然法無全利善變者審其所宜取其大利
略其小害譬之治病診其脉理調和其元
氣已其大痼而後一指之痛一癬之害是
故一不勝而再勝善戰者趨之矣利十而
===
害一良賈爭之矣十人言便而一人言不
便從十人矣害不勝利猶利也然法雖利
用法以人非其人不能成功今夫飴美食
也展禽得之以養老盜蹠得之以開閉鍵
飴非有異也故法一也得其人則展禽之
養不得其人則蹠蹻之飴而已矣夫禹貢
之制周官之法往代悠邈時移俗異不可
施之今日愚不敢復云矣
國家賦役之法十年若五年而一舉歲差次
punctuated: 不盡為郡縣，井田之法壞，則不得不開阡陌，時與勢固然也。秦之悖先王者固多，此未可以盡罪秦也。今夫民情，寒則欲火，暑則欲水，燥則欲濕，濕則欲燥，寒暑燥濕相反，其於利民同也。夫變法者，亦以利民耳。然法無全利，善變者審其所宜，取其大利，略其小害。譬之治病，診其脉理，調和其元氣，已其大痼，而後一指之痛、一癬之害。是故一不勝而再勝，善戰者趨之矣；利十而害一，良賈爭之矣；十人言便而一人言不便，從十人矣。害不勝利，猶利也。然法雖利，用法以人，非其人不能成功。今夫飴，美食也，展禽得之以養老，盜蹠得之以開閉鍵，飴非有異也。故法一也，得其人則展禽之養，不得其人則蹠蹻之飴而已矣。夫《禹貢》之制、《周官》之法，往代悠邈，時移俗異，不可施之今日，愚不敢復云矣。國家賦役之法，十年若五年而一舉，歲差次…
translation_en:
…be entirely replaced by commanderies and counties, and once the well-field system had broken down, there was no choice but to open up the field pathways. This was naturally so because of the times and the circumstances. Although there were indeed many ways in which Qin went against the former kings, in this matter the blame cannot be placed entirely upon Qin.

Now, as for the feelings of the people: when cold they desire fire, when hot they desire water, when dry they desire moisture, and when damp they desire dryness. Cold and heat, dryness and dampness are opposites, yet they are the same in benefiting the people. Those who reform the laws do so simply to benefit the people as well. Yet no law is wholly beneficial. Those skilled at reform examine what is appropriate, seizing upon the great benefits and overlooking the minor harms. It is like treating an illness: one diagnoses the courses of the pulse, harmonizes the vital氣 (yuanqi), and cures the major chronic malady, leaving for last the pain of a single finger or the harm of a single patch of ringworm. Therefore, if one suffers a single defeat but wins twice, a skilled commander will pursue it; if there are ten parts of profit to one part of harm, a good merchant will vie for it; if ten men say something is convenient and one man says it is inconvenient, one follows the ten men. As long as the harm does not outweigh the benefit, it is still a benefit.

Even so, although a law may be beneficial, implementing the law depends on the men; without the right men, success cannot be achieved. Now, malt sugar is a fine food: when Zhan Qin (柳下惠 Liuxia Hui) obtained it, he used it to nourish the elderly; when Robber Zhi (Dao Zhi 盜蹠) obtained it, he used it to unfasten bolts and locks—and yet the malt sugar itself was no different. Thus, the law is one and the same: if one gets the right men, it is the nourishment of a Zhan Qin; if one does not get the right men, it is nothing more than the malt sugar of a Robber Zhi or a Zhuang Qiao (莊蹻).

As for the institutions of the Tribute of Yu (Yugong) and the laws of the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan), those past eras are remote and distant; times have changed and customs differ, so they cannot be applied today, and this foolish one dare not speak of them again.

In our Dynasty's system of taxation and labor service, a general assessment is conducted once every ten or five years, and each year [households] are graded in sequence…

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
里甲戶考其民數之盈縮以賦於民民得
番休孰謂不便民哉行之旣久豪民俠夫
私其吏胥變亂藏籍以逃征繇而又賦斂
繁多科求時出愚民不知吏因緣多取爲
姦閭閻粍矣有司患之於是請歲通計其
所入而總賦之戶頒之以所賦之數而罷
前法問之父老皆曰便百姓人人知所宜
入當數而止一約法畫一吏牘大損而狙
公之弊巳二豪猾不得規走輕重而賦役
===
均三公家易催征四子弟得罷歸農五胥
隸受其直於官不得多取六此六者今法
之利也其言不便者諸供億悉在官官率
取之市人或給之直不當又百姓已罷歸
有私役之者所頒賦數間爲吏所匿山谷
窮民不能盡見因而多賦之蓋聞之人言
云然今上官督之密吏凜凜奉法事恐不
然即有之可百邑之一二邑中數戶而止
耳然此非法之弊也謂宜博選良吏而諸
punctuated: 里甲戶，考其民數之盈縮，以賦於民，民得番休，孰謂不便民哉？行之旣久，豪民俠夫私其吏胥，變亂藏籍，以逃征繇。而又賦斂繁多，科求時出，愚民不知，吏因緣多取爲姦，閭閻粍矣。有司患之，於是請歲通計其所入而總賦之，戶頒之以所賦之數，而罷前法。問之父老，皆曰便：百姓人人知所宜入，當數而止，一；約法畫一，吏牘大損，而狙公之弊巳，二；豪猾不得規走輕重，而賦役均，三；公家易催征，四；子弟得罷歸農，五；胥隸受其直於官，不得多取，六。此六者，今法之利也。其言不便者：諸供億悉在官，官率取之市人，或給之直不當；又百姓已罷歸，有私役之者；所頒賦數，間爲吏所匿，山谷窮民不能盡見，因而多賦之。蓋聞之人言云然，今上官督之密，吏凜凜奉法，事恐不然，即有之，可百邑之一二，邑中數戶而止耳。然此非法之弊也，謂宜博選良吏，而諸
translation_en: … the households of the community-tithing system (lijia), examining the increase and decrease in the population in order to levy taxes upon the people, so that the people could take turns resting—who would say this was not convenient for the people? Yet after it had been practiced for a long time, powerful commoners and unruly men colluded privately with the subofficial functionaries and runners, altering and throwing into confusion the stored registers in order to evade tax and corvée service. Moreover, taxes and exactions became numerous and varied, and special requisitions were frequently issued. The ignorant people did not know better, and the subofficial functionaries took advantage of the situation to extract extra amounts and commit fraud, so that the village communities were depleted. The authorities were troubled by this, and thereupon requested each year to calculate comprehensively the total revenue due and levy it as a single combined tax, distributing to each household a notice of the amount it was to pay, while abolishing the former method. When one asks the village elders about it, they all say it is convenient: First, every single one of the common people knows what they ought to pay, and once they meet that amount it stops. Second, the simplified regulations are uniform, official paperwork is greatly reduced, and the abuse of tricky manipulation (jugong) is ended. Third, powerful and cunning people cannot scheme to shift burdens between light and heavy, so that taxes and corvée are equalized. Fourth, it is easy for the public administration to press for collection. Fifth, the young men are released from service to return to farming. Sixth, the petty clerks and runners receive their wages from the government and cannot extract extra amounts. These six points are the advantages of the present method. As for those who say it is inconvenient: since all provisioning and supplies now rest with the officials, the officials generally procure them from market merchants, sometimes paying them an inadequate price; furthermore, although the common people have already been released from service to return home, there are still those who privately conscript them; and the distributed notices of tax amounts are occasionally concealed by subofficial functionaries, so that poor people in mountain valleys cannot all see them, and consequently are overtaxed. Such, it seems, is what one hears people say. Yet nowadays superior officials supervise the matter closely, and subofficial functionaries tremblingly obey the law, so I fear this is not actually the case; even if it does happen, it would amount to no more than one or two out of a hundred districts, and a few households within a district. However, this is not a defect of the law itself. I would say that we ought to broadly select upright officials, and have the various…

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
分部使者與其郡長吏嚴察之則其所捄
也又歳郡縣傜賦悉從所司主賦者考而
書其數頒之簿書上下當留時日有煩細
之病宜令諸郡各審所部賦書而上之司
賦覆覈之轉請得報行之便
國家天下土田十歳而一籍戸進退之以登
民租其初亦稱便焉自賦役繁倍貧人之
産漸入富室畝税不相當豪民黠吏陰移
其田税遁之絶籍負之蚩氓幻不可詰又
===
水濱之民田地亡沒而供不毛之賦若田
賦本重懸致殊科一畝之田而輸一釡者
民以大困而號不均於是有司言均田之
利吏行丈量計其畝辨其壤之上下以輕
重其税蓋以一邑之土受一邑之税可使
戸無羨田人無虚賦豪民無所匿其奸而
貧人解於重負田賦既定徴發不煩又利
公家便矣顧計必屬之良吏乃可施行即
令得良吏又安能一一履畝而親之此其
punctuated:
分部使者與其郡長吏嚴察之，則其所捄也。又歳郡縣傜賦，悉從所司主賦者考而書其數頒之，簿書上下當留時日，有煩細之病。宜令諸郡各審所部賦書，而上之司賦覆覈之，轉請得報行之便。
國家天下土田，十歳而一籍，戸進退之，以登民租，其初亦稱便焉。自賦役繁倍，貧人之産漸入富室，畝税不相當，豪民黠吏陰移其田税，遁之絶籍，負之蚩氓，幻不可詰。又水濱之民，田地亡沒，而供不毛之賦；若田賦本重，懸致殊科，一畝之田而輸一釡者。民以大困，而號不均，於是有司言均田之利。吏行丈量，計其畝，辨其壤之上下，以輕重其税。蓋以一邑之土，受一邑之税，可使戸無羨田，人無虚賦，豪民無所匿其奸，而貧人解於重負。田賦既定，徴發不煩，又利公家，便矣。顧計必屬之良吏，乃可施行；即令得良吏，又安能一一履畝而親之？此其
translation_en:
…circuit-inspecting commissioners and their prefectural senior officials strictly investigate them, this is how it can be remedied. Furthermore, every year the labor services and taxes of prefectures and counties are all examined, recorded in number, and promulgated by the competent fiscal authorities; as the registers pass up and down the bureaucracy, they inevitably take up time and suffer from the flaw of cumbersome pettiness. It would be best to order each prefecture to review the tax registers of its own jurisdiction and submit them to the fiscal commissioner to verify them, and then forward the request to receive approval and put them into effect, which would be convenient.

As for the lands of our Dynasty throughout the realm, once every ten years they are registered, and households are promoted or demoted in grade so as to record the people's taxes; in the beginning this too was praised as convenient. Since taxes and corvée have multiplied, the property of poor people has gradually passed into wealthy households, so that acreage and taxes no longer correspond. Powerful commoners and cunning clerks secretly shift their land taxes, hiding them in extinct household registers or saddling them onto ignorant commoners, with deceptions impossible to untangle. Moreover, people living along the waters have had their fields and lands washed away and submerged, yet still pay taxes on barren nothingness; or else where the land tax was originally heavy, wide disparities have resulted in wildly different rates, with some paying a full fu [6.4 dou] of grain on a single mu of land. The people are thus in great distress and cry out against the inequity, whereupon the authorities speak of the benefits of equalizing land (juntian). Officials carry out cadastral surveys, counting the mu and distinguishing the upper and lower grades of the soil in order to make the taxes lighter or heavier accordingly. The idea is that by having the land of a single county bear the tax quota of that single county, one can ensure that households have no unassessed surplus land and people have no empty tax obligations, that powerful commoners have nowhere to hide their fraud, and that poor people are relieved of heavy burdens. Once the land tax is fixed, collection and requisitions are free of trouble, and it also benefits the state—convenient indeed! Yet the plan must be entrusted to upright officials before it can be carried out; and even supposing one obtains upright officials, how could they possibly tread every single mu in person? Within this…

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
中寧無豪民猾胥相倚爲市以高下其手
而盈縮其數倒置其壤則者乎或不肖之
吏馮法喜怒以快其私臆矣而其弊旣已
見矣又匹夫匹婦傭竭其筋骨誅斥甌簍
於窮谷之隈絕澗之濱以旦夕糊其口者
今皆籍而賦之矣此其初非本賦籍也且
幾何而幷舉之使無所置其錐若是苛也
然此皆吏奉職之過也愚以謂諸言均田
者宜詳見父老咨其利病其無大困於公
===
私者已不可已者屬良吏謹奉行之與之
約諸前所云占田不實者則壤不當者若
吏胥爲奸及擾民者謹督察之不得有一
焉有卽其害百於已矣不可也吏者民之
師帥諸爲吏者宜一以孔子爲師孔子曰
道之以政齊之以刑民免而無恥道之以
德齊之以禮有耻且格又曰君子學道則
愛人小人學道則易使也然而吏治一切
未聞有以禮導民者何其故世俗卑卑沿
punctuated:
中寧無豪民猾胥相倚爲市，以高下其手而盈縮其數、倒置其壤則者乎？或不肖之吏，馮法喜怒以快其私臆矣，而其弊旣已見矣。又匹夫匹婦，傭竭其筋骨，誅斥甌簍於窮谷之隈、絕澗之濱，以旦夕糊其口者，今皆籍而賦之矣。此其初非本賦籍也，且幾何而幷舉之，使無所置其錐，若是苛也？然此皆吏奉職之過也。愚以謂諸言均田者，宜詳見父老，咨其利病，其無大困於公私者，已；不可已者，屬良吏謹奉行之。與之約，諸前所云占田不實者、則壤不當者、若吏胥爲奸及擾民者，謹督察之，不得有一焉。有卽其害百於已矣，不可也。

吏者，民之師帥，諸爲吏者宜一以孔子爲師。孔子曰：「道之以政，齊之以刑，民免而無恥；道之以德，齊之以禮，有耻且格。」又曰：「君子學道則愛人，小人學道則易使也。」然而吏治一切，未聞有以禮導民者，何？其故世俗卑卑，沿
translation_en:
… among them, how could there not be powerful commoners and cunning clerks colluding with one another to make a trade of it, manipulating things with their hands to inflate or shrink the figures and invert the soil-grade classifications? Or perhaps unworthy officials rely on the law to vent their pleasure or anger and gratify their private whims—and the abuses of this have already become apparent! Moreover, ordinary men and women who exhaust their sinews and bones as hired laborers, clearing tiny plots of stony ground in the corners of remote valleys and along the edges of cut-off ravines just to eke out a living from morning to evening, have now all had their land registered and taxed. In the beginning, these were not part of the original tax registers; and how much can they possibly yield that they must be swept up together, leaving these people nowhere to plant even an awl—why be so harsh as this? Yet all these are the faults of officials in executing their duties. In my humble opinion, wherever land equalization is proposed, one ought to interview the local elders in detail and consult them on its advantages and disadvantages. Where there is no great distress to either public or private interests, let the matter drop. Where it cannot be dropped, entrust conscientious officials to carry it out carefully. Make a pact with them that regarding all the aforementioned cases—inaccurate reporting of landholdings, improper grading of soil, or clerks committing fraud and harassing the people—they must carefully supervise and investigate so that not a single instance is allowed to occur. If even one occurs, the harm will be a hundred times worse than not doing it at all; it must not be allowed.

Officials are the teachers and leaders of the people; all who serve as officials ought exclusively to take Confucius as their teacher. Confucius said: "Lead them by means of government measures and regulate them with punishments, and the people will evade them and have no sense of shame. Lead them by means of virtue and regulate them with ritual, and they will have a sense of shame and moreover reform themselves." He also said: "When the gentleman learns the Way, he loves others; when the small man learns the Way, he is easy to employ." And yet in administrative governance across the board, one never hears of anyone guiding the people by means of ritual. Why is this? The reason is that worldly customs are base and petty, following …

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
襲故常而莫之知卽知者又見謂闊遠未
遑也故曰下士聞道大笑之此之謂也曩
吾見郡縣有設爲鄉約敎民者嘗過其里
閭見其父老子弟衣冠言動率循循能遵
用其敎矣故知敎不可已民在所道當少
漸積效實耳以爲虛文而罷之謂其不可
猝道而棄之然則禮敎之興無時巳
高皇帝著爲訓諭歲時令長老諷誦以鐸徇於
里巷固此道也宜令郡縣因
===
高帝訓辭稍爲之約擇里中賢者爲之長而禮
焉使月旦朢集其里之少長敎之孝弟德
義習以禮讓察其善否某也善指其事而
揚之某也過指其事而敎之如此可使人
人自勸重爲不善而俗大創也而又稍以
朱子所著冠婚喪祭儀禮與父老約行之
行之不止將斌斌禮義之俗太平之跡可
睹矣第恐吏不暇行行不實又重姍咲耳古
者敎化行而法令備民出入相友守朢相
punctuated: 襲故常而莫之知，卽知者，又見謂闊遠未遑也。故曰：「下士聞道，大笑之。」此之謂也。曩吾見郡縣有設爲鄉約敎民者，嘗過其里閭，見其父老子弟，衣冠言動，率循循能遵用其敎矣。故知敎不可已，民在所道，當少漸積效實耳。以爲虛文而罷之，謂其不可猝道而棄之，然則禮敎之興，無時巳。高皇帝著爲訓諭，歲時令長老諷誦，以鐸徇於里巷，固此道也。宜令郡縣因高帝訓辭，稍爲之約，擇里中賢者爲之長而禮焉。使月旦朢集其里之少長，敎之孝弟德義，習以禮讓，察其善否。某也善，指其事而揚之；某也過，指其事而敎之。如此，可使人人自勸，重爲不善，而俗大創也。而又稍以朱子所著冠婚喪祭儀禮，與父老約行之。行之不止，將斌斌禮義之俗、太平之跡可睹矣。第恐吏不暇行，行不實，又重姍咲耳。古者敎化行而法令備，民出入相友，守朢相
translation_en: …follow old routines without knowing any better; and even those who do know dismiss it as impractical and say they have no time for it. Hence the saying, "When the inferior man hears of the Way, he laughs aloud at it"—this is what it means. In the past, I saw prefectures and counties that established community compacts (xiangyue) to instruct the people. When I passed through their villages and lanes, I observed that the elders and youths, in their dress, speech, and conduct, generally followed the instructions in an orderly manner. Thus we know that instruction must not cease: the people depend on how they are guided, and one need only accumulate results gradually over time. If one abolishes it as empty formality, or abandons it on the grounds that they cannot be guided all at once, then the revival of ritual instruction will never come to pass. When the Exalted Emperor (Gao Huangdi, i.e., Emperor Taizu) composed his instructive edicts and ordered the elders at seasonal intervals to recite them, shaking a wooden-clapper bell through the village lanes, it was precisely this Way. Prefectures and counties should be ordered to draw upon the Exalted Emperor's instructive words to formulate concise compacts, selecting worthy men in the villages to serve as their heads and treating them with ritual courtesy. Have them assemble the young and old of their village on the first and fifteenth of each month to instruct them in filial piety, brotherly respect, moral virtue, and righteousness, accustom them to ritual propriety and deference, and examine their good and bad conduct. When a certain person does good, point out his deed and praise him; when a certain person errs, point out his deed and instruct him. In this way, everyone can be made to encourage himself, hesitate gravely to do wrong, and customs will be greatly reformed. Furthermore, one should gradually introduce the rituals of capping, marriage, mourning, and sacrifice compiled by Master Zhu (Zhu Xi), agreeing with the village elders to put them into practice. If this is practiced unceasingly, then refined customs of ritual and righteousness and the traces of great peace will soon be visible. I only fear that officials will not take the time to carry it out, or will carry it out without sincerity, and once again incur heavy ridicule. In antiquity, moral transformation was practiced and laws and ordinances were complete; the people befriended one another in their comings and goings, and in keeping watch and ward they mutually…

title: 萬曆七年浙江鄉試錄
text:
助故風俗美厚無盜賊之患今天下憂於
盜矣夫盜賊者此其人不自天降自地出
也由四方遊俠得容於鄉里而吾遊惰暴
桀子弟得出而爲之黨也及於緩急又不
相救則保甲之法不行也宋王介甫嘗爲
保甲之法其法十家爲保五十家爲大保
十大保爲都保而擇衆所服者爲都保正
若副聽其自置弓矢習武藝而自相糾察
摘其奸宄故里閈不敢犯禁觸罪雖有盜
===
===
蹠企足之奸不得逞焉安石新法病民而
玆法良善實可施行今世多倣行之然上
下相蒙虛文耳無益於俗亦未徧行也宜
如其法立之長使戶計其丁男書之而時
察其出入以禁切其子弟且使姦人無所
容否者十家坐之約里中盜至衆共救之
不如約者告于官當以罪如是而姦安從
生何憂盜乎而愚見今之保甲法不然直
榜之門爲官長容過則藏之矣故曰在人
punctuated: 助，故風俗美厚，無盜賊之患。今天下憂於盜矣。夫盜賊者，此其人不自天降、自地出也。由四方遊俠得容於鄉里，而吾遊惰暴桀子弟得出而爲之黨也。及於緩急，又不相救，則保甲之法不行也。宋王介甫嘗爲保甲之法，其法：十家爲保，五十家爲大保，十大保爲都保，而擇衆所服者爲都保正若副。聽其自置弓矢，習武藝，而自相糾察，摘其奸宄，故里閈不敢犯禁觸罪。雖有盜蹠企足之奸，不得逞焉。安石新法病民，而玆法良善，實可施行。今世多倣行之，然上下相蒙，虛文耳，無益於俗，亦未徧行也。宜如其法，立之長，使戶計其丁男書之，而時察其出入，以禁切其子弟，且使姦人無所容，否者十家坐之。約里中盜至，衆共救之；不如約者告于官，當以罪。如是，而姦安從生？何憂盜乎？而愚見今之保甲法不然，直榜之門，爲官長容，過則藏之矣。故曰：在人
translation_en: …aid in mutual defense, and thus customs were virtuous and generous, free from the scourge of bandits and thieves. Today, the empire is troubled by banditry. Yet as for bandits and thieves, such people do not drop from heaven or spring from the earth. They arise because wandering vigilantes from all quarters are harbored in the villages, and our own idle, violent, and unruly youths are able to go out and join their gangs. Moreover, when emergencies arise, people do not come to one another's aid, which is because the mutual security (baojia) system is not enforced. In the Song dynasty, Wang Jiefu (Wang Anshi 王安石) once established the baojia system. Under his regulations, ten households formed a guard (bao), fifty households formed a large guard (dabao), and ten large guards formed a superior guard (dubao), with those respected by the multitude chosen as Superior Guard Chiefs (dubao zheng) or Deputies (fu).
